Source. `Parse_InitExpr()` materializes a temporary `M3Compilation` over the current data-segment initializer. The nearby comment says this path "just walks the wasm bytecode to find the end", so later `Compile_BlockStatements()` iterations read directly from the attacker-supplied init-expression bytes in `compilation.wasm`.

A later crashing iteration of the init-expression walk decodes the next attacker-controlled byte from `o->wasm` into local variable `opcode` and stores it to `*o_value`. The exact 108-byte witness contains no `0xFC` bytes anywhere, so this path never takes the widening branch that would build an extended opcode; the next step therefore receives an ordinary single-byte opcode (`opcode >> 8 == 0x00`). Earlier noncrashing iterations and recursive call plumbing are omitted because they only advance the same byte stream to this later decode site.

Root cause. Because step 2 never builds an extended opcode for this witness, `GetOpInfo()` dispatches on the ordinary-opcode arm and returns `&c_operations[opcode]`. That lookup uses the attacker-derived byte directly as an array index and does not check `opcode < M3_COUNT_OF(c_operations)`, so an out-of-range opcode yields a non-NULL pointer outside the real table.

The only guard after `GetOpInfo()` rejects a NULL pointer, not an out-of-range one. Because step 3 returns a non-NULL pointer value even when it aliases memory beyond the opcode table, this check succeeds and control falls through to the dereference site.
Sink. `Compile_BlockStatements()` dereferences the unchecked pointer from step 3 to read its `compiler` field. That first field read is the saved AddressSanitizer global-buffer-overflow at line 2210.
